{{Short description|Tree graph with exactly one vertex of degree >2}}
[[File:Starlike graph.svg|thumb|upright=0.75|A starlike tree]]
In the mathematical subdiscipline of [[graph theory]], a [[tree (graph theory)|tree]] is said to be '''starlike''' if it has exactly one vertex of [[degree (graph theory)|degree]] greater than&nbsp;2. This high-degree vertex is the '''root''' (or '''central vertex'''), and a starlike tree can be seen as resulting from attaching to this central vertex at least three [[path graph|linear graph]]s (paths). Starlike trees are also referred to as '''spider graphs'''.

== Definition ==
More formally, let <math>k \geq 3</math> and <math>n_1, \ldots, n_k \geq 1</math> be positive integers. The starlike tree <math>S(n_1, \ldots, n_k)</math> is a tree <math>T</math> with a central vertex <math>v</math> of degree <math>k</math> such that <math>T \setminus v \cong P_{n_1} \cup \cdots \cup P_{n_k}</math>, where <math>P_t</math> denotes the [[path graph]] on <math>t</math> vertices, and every neighbor of <math>v</math> in <math>T</math> has degree one or two. The total number of vertices in <math>S(n_1, \ldots, n_k)</math> is <math>n_1 + \cdots + n_k + 1</math>. The simplest starlike tree is the [[star graph]] <math>S_k = S(1, \ldots, 1)</math> with <math>k</math> branches of length one.<ref name="Oboudi2018">{{cite journal | last=Oboudi | first=Mohammad Reza | title=On the eigenvalues and spectral radius of starlike trees | journal=Aequationes Mathematicae | volume=92 | issue=4 | pages=683–694 | date=August 2018 | doi=10.1007/s00010-017-0533-4 | url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/322685193_On_the_eigenvalues_and_spectral_radius_of_starlike_trees | issn=0001-9054}}</ref>

== Properties ==
=== Spectral properties ===
Two finite starlike trees are [[isospectral]], i.e. their [[discrete Laplace operator|graph Laplacians]] have the same spectra, if and only if they are [[graph isomorphism|isomorphic]].<ref name="LepovicGutman">M. Lepovic, I. Gutman (2001). [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0012365X01001698 No starlike trees are cospectral.]</ref> The graph Laplacian has always only one eigenvalue equal or greater than&nbsp;4.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Nakatsukasa | first1=Yuji | last2=Saito | first2=Naoki | last3=Woei | first3=Ernest | title=Mysteries around the Graph Laplacian Eigenvalue 4 | journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications | volume=438 | issue=8 | pages=3231–46 | date=April 2013 | doi=10.1016/j.laa.2012.12.012 | arxiv=1112.4526}}</ref>

=== Spectral radius bounds ===
The [[spectral radius]] of a starlike tree (the largest eigenvalue of its [[adjacency matrix]]) can be bounded in terms of its maximum degree <math>\Delta</math>. For starlike trees <math>S(n_1, \ldots, n_k)</math> with <math>k \geq 4</math> and <math>n_1, \ldots, n_k \geq 2</math>, the spectral radius <math>\lambda_1</math> satisfies:<ref name="Oboudi2018" />

:<math>\frac{k-1}{\sqrt{k-2}} < \lambda_1(S(n_1, \ldots, n_k)) < \frac{k}{\sqrt{k-1}}</math>

or equivalently, in terms of the maximum degree <math>\Delta = k</math>:

:<math>\frac{\Delta - 1}{\sqrt{\Delta - 2}} < \lambda_1 < \frac{\Delta}{\sqrt{\Delta - 1}}</math>

These bounds show that the spectral radius of such starlike trees is asymptotically <math>\sqrt{\Delta}</math> as the maximum degree grows large.

For specific cases:<ref name="Oboudi2018" />
* If <math>k = 3</math> and all branches have length 1, then <math>\lambda_1 = \sqrt{3}</math>
* If <math>k = 3</math> and all branches have length 2, then <math>\lambda_1 = 2</math>
* If <math>k \geq 4</math> and all branches have length 1 (i.e., the tree is a star <math>S_{k+1}</math>), then <math>\lambda_1 = \sqrt{k}</math>

=== Eigenvalues in the interval (−2, 2) ===
The eigenvalues of starlike trees have been characterized with respect to the interval <math>(-2, 2)</math>. A starlike tree <math>S(n_1, n_2, n_3)</math> with three branches has all of its eigenvalues in the open interval <math>(-2, 2)</math> if and only if it is isomorphic to one of the following:
* <math>S(1, 1, m)</math> for any positive integer <math>m</math>
* <math>S(1, 2, 2)</math>, <math>S(1, 2, 3)</math>, or <math>S(1, 2, 4)</math>

For starlike trees with four or more branches <math>(k \geq 4)</math>, at least one eigenvalue lies outside the interval <math>(-2, 2)</math>.<ref name="Oboudi2018" />

=== Topological indices ===

Vertex-degree-based topological indices are molecular descriptors defined as <math>TI(G) = \sum_{1 \leq i \leq j \leq n-1} m_{ij}(G) \varphi_{ij}</math>, where <math>m_{ij}(G)</math> is the number of edges between vertices of degree <math>i</math> and degree <math>j</math>, and the values <math>\varphi_{ij}</math> determine the specific index. Examples include the [[Randić index]], [[Zagreb index|first Zagreb index]], [[harmonic index]], and [[atom-bond connectivity index]].<ref name="BetancurCruzRada2015">{{cite journal | last1=Betancur | first1=Clara | last2=Cruz | first2=Roberto | last3=Rada | first3=Juan | title=Vertex-degree-based topological indices over starlike trees | journal=Discrete Applied Mathematics | volume=185 | pages=18–25 | date=2015 | doi=10.1016/j.dam.2014.12.021 | issn=0166-218X}}</ref>

For a starlike tree <math>X</math> with <math>n</math> vertices and central degree <math>k</math>, any such index satisfies <math>TI(X) = k_1 P_k + k Q_k + (n-1)\varphi_{22}</math>, where <math>k_1</math> is the number of branches of length 1, <math>P_k = \varphi_{1k} + \varphi_{22} - \varphi_{12} - \varphi_{2k}</math>, and <math>Q_k = \varphi_{12} + \varphi_{2k} - 2\varphi_{22}</math>. This shows that the index value depends primarily on the number of unit-length branches.<ref name="BetancurCruzRada2015" />

Among all starlike trees on <math>n</math> vertices, the extremal values are typically attained by the star graph <math>S(1, 1, \ldots, 1)</math> with <math>n-1</math> branches and the tree <math>S(2, 2, n-5)</math>. For indices where <math>P_k \leq 0</math> for all <math>k \geq 3</math> (including the Randić, harmonic, sum-connectivity, geometric-arithmetic, and augmented Zagreb indices), the star graph attains the minimum and <math>S(2,2,n-5)</math> attains the maximum. The reverse holds for indices where <math>P_k \geq 0</math> (including the first Zagreb, Albertson, and atom-bond connectivity indices).<ref name="BetancurCruzRada2015" />
